name: OPA189IDR
title: 36-V zero-drift, 14-MHz, low-noise rail-to-rail output operational amplifiers (single, dual, quad)
summary: OPA189 (single), OPA2189 (dual) and OPA4189 (quad) are chopper-stabilized precision op amps running from 4.5 V to 36 V. The single holds 3 µV maximum offset and 0.02 µV/°C maximum drift, with 5.2 nV/√Hz flat noise, 14-MHz gain bandwidth and 20 V/µs slew. The CMOS input reaches the negative rail and has no anti-parallel clamp diodes, so a multiplexer can switch it between widely different voltages without loading the source; the output swings rail to rail.
key_figures: 1.3 mA typ, 1.7 mA max per amplifier

circuits.title: 25-kHz low-pass filter
circuits.description: Second-order multiple-feedback low-pass filter with an inverting gain of 5 V/V, a 25-kHz corner and a Chebyshev response peaking 3 dB in the passband. R1 and C2 form the first pole at the input; R4 returns the output to the R1-C2 node and sets the gain against R1; R3 and C5 close the integrator round the amplifier. The noninverting input is grounded.

circuits.title: Discrete instrumentation amplifier with attenuation for a 3.3-V ADC
circuits.description: Two OPAx189 followers with gain form the high-impedance, high-voltage front end of a three-resistor instrumentation amplifier: RP and RN feed each output back to its inverting input and RG joins the two inverting inputs, giving a differential gain of 1 + 2·10 kΩ/500 Ω = 41. An INA159 difference amplifier on 5 V takes VOUTP and VOUTN, scales the difference by 1/5 and offsets it by half of Ref 1 (tied to 5 V), so VOUT = VDIFF × 41/5 + Ref 1/2 suits a 3.3-V or 5-V converter. The amplifiers run from ±15 V; the test sources ride on a 10-V common-mode level.

circuits.title: Bridge amplifier
circuits.description: A four-resistor bridge excited from VEX feeds a difference amplifier on a single 5-V supply. The bridge's right node drives the inverting input, where R1 closes the loop from the output; the left node goes to the noninverting input, which a second resistor references to VREF. The bridge's bottom node is ground.

circuits.title: Low-side current monitor
circuits.description: The load current returns to ground through a 100-mΩ shunt; the amplifier, on a single 15-V supply, amplifies the shunt voltage noninverting with a gain of 1 + 20 kΩ/100 Ω = 201. A load current of 0 A to 500 mA gives 0 V to 10 V out, 1 V per 49.75 mA. CF across RF limits the bandwidth. Changing the shunt or the gain moves the range.

circuits.title: Programmable power supply
circuits.description: A 16-bit DAC8581 sets a ±5-V input; the OPAx189 on ±15 V drives an OPA548 power amplifier on ±30 V through R3, and the whole chain is closed round the OPA548 output by R4 and R1 so the output is five times the DAC voltage, ±25 V. The OPAx189 compares the DAC voltage with the R4-R1 tap through R2, so its precision sets the output's; C2 round the OPAx189 and C1 across R4 compensate the composite loop for capacitive and current loads.

circuits.title: RTD amplifier with linearization
circuits.description: A REF5050 makes 5 V from 15 V. R1 feeds a Pt100 RTD from that reference and the RTD voltage drives the noninverting input; R2 and R4 bias the inverting input and R3 sets the gain from the output. R5 from the output back to the RTD node adds excitation that rises with the output, straightening the RTD's curve. The output is 0 V at 0 °C and 5 V at 200 °C. Each side of the reference has 1 µF to ground.

circuits.title: 24-bit differential load cell or strain gauge signal conditioning
circuits.description: A 5-V excited load cell drives two OPAx189 in a two-amplifier instrumentation amplifier on a single 15-V supply, gain G = 1 + 2·RF/RG = 1 + 2·10 kΩ/50 Ω = 401. Each amplifier has RF with CF in parallel from its output to its inverting input, and RG joins the two inverting inputs; both outputs sit at VEX/2. R1, R2 and C1 to C3 filter the outputs into the ADS1225 24-bit delta-sigma converter's AINP1 and AINN1. The converter's reference is the load cell's sense lines, through the trace resistances, filtered by C4 to C6. A host drives START and SCLK and reads DRDY/DOUT.

circuits.title: EMIRR IN+ test configuration
circuits.description: The amplifier runs as a unity-gain buffer at 25 °C ambient. An RF source (0-V dc bias, unmodulated carrier, 201-point logarithmic frequency sweep) reaches the noninverting input through a 50-Ω transmission line. The output passes a low-pass filter to a digital multimeter that samples and averages the dc offset the RF produces. The supplies carry 0.1-µF and 10-µF decoupling.

circuits.title: Noninverting amplifier with input overstress protection
circuits.description: A noninverting stage (RI to ground, RF from the output) driving RL, with VIN reaching +IN through RS. With VIN 500 mV above V+, the upper input steering diode conducts and the input current ID flows into the V+ supply; RS of about 5 kΩ limits it. A TVS from each supply pin to ground, its minimum breakdown above the supply and below 40 V, clamps a supply that cannot sink that current.

circuits.title: Difference amplifier (layout example)
circuits.description: A four-resistor difference amplifier: R1 takes IN− to the inverting input and R3 returns the output to it; R2 takes IN+ to the noninverting input and R4 ties that input to ground. Each supply pin has two bypass capacitors to ground, C3 and C4 on +V, C1 and C2 on −V. The board layout keeps R1 to R4 and the capacitors close to the pins, with ground pours round the input pairs.

operation.text: OPA189, OPA2189 and OPA4189 hold one, two and four amplifiers. The single comes in SOIC-8, VSSOP-8 and SOT-23-5, the dual in SOIC-8 and VSSOP-8, the quad in SOIC-14 and TSSOP-14. Every version is specified from −40 °C to +125 °C. Offset and drift limits differ between the single, the OPA2189ID and the OPA2189IDGK/OPA4189IPW.

A zero-drift (chopper) amplifier with a periodic self-calibration: near-zero offset and offset drift across temperature and time, no 1/f noise, and low distortion below the chopping frequency. Inside are input protection switches, three gain stages with a feed-forward path, a ripple-reduction feedback loop and a slew-boost circuit. It is stable at unity gain and the output swings rail to rail.

Runs from 4.5 V (±2.25 V) to 36 V (±18 V), single or split; the rails need not be symmetrical. Above 40 V across the supply pins the part can be destroyed. Below ±2.5 V the input common-mode range does not include mid-supply. There is one operating mode, active whenever the supply exceeds 4.5 V.
An input driven past the common-mode range does not flip the output to the opposite rail: the output stays at the rail the input calls for.

The chopper's input switches inject charge, which shows up as brief spikes in input bias current. They are too short to be amplified directly but can reach the output through the feedback network; an RC low-pass after the amplifier removes them.

The inputs carry built-in EMI filters. EMIRR IN+ is measured with RF on the noninverting input, 10 MHz to 6 GHz; it is 48.4 dB at 400 MHz rising to 95.5 dB at 5 GHz. The inverting input, built symmetrically, behaves nearly the same, and the dual and quad match the single closely.

There are no anti-parallel clamp diodes across the inputs. A switched input stage keeps the input impedance high while a large differential voltage is applied, so a channel switch in a multiplexer or a large step does not pull current from the source or upset its RC filter; settling stays fast. The part can be run as a comparator. The absolute maximum common-mode and differential limits, taken against the supplies, still hold.

Steering diodes run from every input and the output to internal supply rails, which meet at an edge-triggered absorption clamp that fires above the operating voltage and below breakdown. They stay off in normal use. An input more than about 500 mV beyond a rail turns a steering diode on; limit input current to 10 mA, for instance with a series resistor near 5 kΩ. If the supply cannot sink that current, the input can lift the rail past its limit; a zener or TVS on each supply pin, rated above the operating supply, prevents it. With the supplies at 0 V and low impedance, an input signal can drive large current through the diodes; with them high impedance, the input can power the part.

With a CMOS input, current noise (165 fA/√Hz) is negligible at any practical source resistance and the 5.2 nV/√Hz voltage noise dominates. Against the bipolar OPA211, the OPAx189 has lower total noise once the source resistance exceeds 3.6 kΩ. Total noise is the root-sum-square of the amplifier's voltage noise, its current noise times the source and feedback resistances, and the thermal noise of those resistors.

Junctions of dissimilar metals in the input path act as thermocouples and can produce 0.1 µV/°C or more. Keep both inputs' junctions at the same temperature: use metals of low thermoelectric coefficient, keep heat sources away, and shield the amplifier and input parts from air currents such as fans.

Place a 0.1-µF low-ESR ceramic capacitor from each supply pin to ground, close to the part; on a single supply one capacitor from V+ to ground is enough. Noisy or high-impedance supplies need it most.

Keep analog and digital grounds apart and watch where ground current flows; a ground plane helps with heat and EMI. Run input traces short and away from supply and output traces, crossing noisy traces at right angles if they must cross. Keep the feedback and gain resistors tight against the inverting pin so its stray capacitance stays small. A low-impedance driven guard ring round sensitive traces cuts leakage. Pour ground round the input pairs and avoid vias in the bypass capacitor connections.
Clean the board after assembly. Moisture absorbed into the plastic package can shift a precision part's performance; after aqueous cleaning, bake the assembly at 85 °C for 30 minutes.
All orderable versions are MSL level 2 with a 260 °C peak reflow and RoHS compliant. OPA189 in SOIC and SOT-23 has NiPdAu leads, OPA189 in VSSOP NiPdAuAg, and the OPA2189 and OPA4189 tin (Sn).
